Designer portal · The document surface · UX review · 13 August 2026

The book won’t close.

The doc is one beautiful route asked to be seven documents. In project phase it tells the designer three different things about where the job is and never says which one is true. In install — the week that actually costs money — it composes almost nothing new, and lets a book close with an uninstalled, uninvoiced $3,200 chair still on the page. The fixes are compositional, not schematic: nothing below asks for new data.

What was walked
A full creation→install attempt on a fresh engagement, plus read-only passes over four live docs at every phase: project, install, care.
Where
Production — app.patina.cloud, signed in as kody@kochaver.com, Middle Studio.
When
Thu 13 Aug 2026 — two independent walking sessions, which reproduced each other’s worst finding without coordinating. Every screenshot here is a real capture from that account.
What it produced
Six themes, a friction timeline with four new HIGH findings, one hard wall, and three proposed compositions.
02

Before the critique

How the doc is built

There is exactly one document route — /doc/[id]. No tabs, no sub-routes, no /schedule or /budget page. Phase never changes the URL. A single database view collapses four different engagement shapes into one string, active_section, and that string decides what the page mounts. Everything the designer experiences as “a phase” is that one branch.

Two consequences carry the whole critique. First: because everything is one page, hierarchy is the only navigation the designer has — fourteen bands deep, with no tabs and no sub-routes. Second: install does not add a mode, it subtracts bands. Read the two columns against each other — crossing into install removes the authority band, the budget grid, the authorizations ledger, the room grouping and every FF&E action, and replaces them with a single line of text.

03

The heart of it

Six ways the doc comes apart

T1 · The orienting devices contradict each other

CriticalConfidence high

Four things on one page claim to know where the job is, each computed differently, with no arbiter: the header chip, the left rail, the schedule caption, and the desk card that sent you here. On Winky the rail says the project is live in week two while the caption directly above a fully-composed six-milestone schedule says no phase is configured at all.

Rail: Project — ACTIVE · WEEK 2  ·  header: PROJECT · ACTIVE WORK · GATE
Caption, eleven hundred pixels lower: NO ACTIVE OR DELAYED PHASE IS CONFIGURED

A document is trusted because it is one record. Two lines disagreeing turns it into widgets sharing a URL — and a designer who cannot trust the page goes back to her spreadsheet, which is the only competitor that matters.

And the way back lies too

From Winkys, opening THE SCAN lands on the room at /room/fa361ed4…?from=document. Its ← THE DOCUMENT breadcrumb does not return you: it follows the room’s canonical document link rather than where you actually came from, and lands on a different project entirely — a second, near-identical “Kody Winky” job with different dates, a different budget and a different week. A designer mid-thought is silently teleported to another job, on a control whose whole promise is “back.”

Note the duplicate itself: two near-identical Kody Winky projects exist. That corroborates the duplicate rows already seen in the People room, now from the document side.

One more, weaker: on Harper Vale the page’s single most prominent call to action — RESOLVE THE SCHEDULE, under Two installs collide — week of Nov 30 — produced no navigation, no scroll, no modal and no visible change when clicked. Single trial, no network correlation — medium confidence, and worth one deliberate re-test before anyone files it.

Principle violated  ·  status legibility / single source of truth; and navigation must be reversible — “back” must mean back.

Fix direction

Elect the schedule spine as the canonical status organ. Header chip and desk cards render its output verbatim — never a second computation. Breadcrumbs follow the held document, not a record’s canonical link.

T2 · Install is not a real mode

CriticalConfidence high

Install does not compose a mode. Walked side by side against a project-phase doc, install subtracts: the Design Authority band, the Working Budget grid and the Authorizations & Trade Scopes ledger are all simply gone, the room grouping is gone, every FF&E action is gone, and the entire furnishings schedule collapses into one line of caption text with no controls on it. The only unfolded working surface left is the Care task list — which belongs to the phase after this one.

So the most operationally distinct week in the engagement gets the least distinct composition, and the least capable one. Install’s unit of work is a room and a day; the page’s unit of work is a line item and a decision. Punch — generated on the walk, gating final payment — isn’t even a band; it lives as coordination rows inside the schedule.

Everything install has to say about seventeen pieces of furniture, in full:
Install    0 OF 1 INSTALLED  ·  BILL 1 UNINVOICED

Then closing is a state change rather than a gate. Harper Vale is a closed book with an uninstalled, uninvoiced $3,200 custom reading chair still displayed on it.

The book closed Jul 31.
Install  ·  0 OF 1 INSTALLED  ·  BILL 1 UNINVOICED
UX Audit — Custom reading chair  ·  SPECIFIED  ·  $3,200

Principle violated  ·  mode fidelity / task-form matching; and the missing forcing function — a state that must not persist needs a stop, not a silent field.

Fix direction

Give install its own composition: lead with room-by-room state, promote punch to a peer band, make close a checklist gate, and defer Care until that gate clears.

T3 · Four financial instruments, no hierarchy

MajorConfidence high

Design Authority, Working Budget, Authorizations & Trade Scopes, and The accounts are four different kinds of thing — a permission, a plan, a commitment, a ledger — standing in a strict dependency chain. The doc renders them as equal siblings in near-identical typography, one after another, so the chain is invisible and the reader has to reconstruct it every visit.

The rendering also disagrees with itself: an accounts strip reading zero sits a screen below a room line that has already released nearly fourteen thousand dollars.

DESIGN AUTHORITY · ACTIVE   $100,000 authorized · $0 accrued · $0 pending · $100,000 remaining
Living   0 OF 2 UNDERWAY  ·  $13,772 RELEASED  ·  $0 NOT YET
The accounts · this project   $0 BUDGET · $0 COMMITTED   STUDIO EYES ONLY

Principle violated  ·  visual hierarchy must express semantic hierarchy.

Fix direction

Nest all four into one money region: one dominant headline figure, three subordinate tiers reading in dependency order — authority → plan → committed → moved.

T4 · No fleet view — the desk answers a different question

CriticalConfidence high

There is no surface anywhere that lists every engagement with its phase. The desk is a triage inbox — Good morning. and NEEDS YOUR HAND · 7 — answering “what is on fire.” The doc answers “this job.” The question a studio principal actually opens the laptop with, what is the state of my book, has no page. “Show me everything in install” has no path at all.

This is also why the system tolerates hollow projects: nothing anywhere ever renders the sentence “three active projects have no schedule composed.” The desk cheerfully pushes an overdue invoice on Test Walker — a project whose schedule is entirely unconfigured and which has no decision lead. Downstream consequences are enforced; the upstream cause is invisible. And the desk’s one breadth affordance, REVEAL 3 MORE FOLIOS ↓, produced no visible change when clicked.

Principle violated  ·  overview first, then zoom and filter — the doc offers detail with no overview above it.

Fix direction

Add a roster tier above the doc — every engagement by phase — and reposition the desk as the exceptions view over that list rather than the only list.

T5 · Empty modules erode the document metaphor

MajorConfidence high

Mood boards and the plan room were empty on every project inspected, regardless of maturity — on the best-populated live job and on a fully closed one alike. The empty states themselves are lovely and on-brand, which is the problem: they are undifferentiated, so emptiness stops being a signal. A budget band with nothing entered renders as a broken sentence. And a phase input is still offered after the phase has passed.

Start the project’s visual direction — on a week-two job and on a closed book, identically.
The plan room — no drawings filed yet.
Budget band, unset: BAND $ from – to $0
Still offered after Completion: Name a phase…

Four chapters of the bound book are blank in every copy ever printed. That makes the binding read as scaffolding rather than as a record, and an interface that keeps offering authoring affordances never reads as finished.

Principle violated  ·  progressive disclosure; empty states must carry meaning.

Fix direction

Let composition respond to phase and content: never-populated bands collapse to one quiet line, and authoring affordances retire when their phase passes.

T6 · The document leaks its own machinery

MajorConfidence high

Internal taxonomy is printed into the reading surface, in the same uppercase mono register the doc uses for legitimate status — so it reads as consequential, and with no remedy offered, it reads as an error the designer caused.

2 ACTIVE PHASES NOT CLASSIFIED TO A CANONICAL STAGE
DERIVED FROM THE PROJECT SCHEDULE · NO TEMPLATE PROVENANCE RECORDED
SECTION GUIDANCE · NO PROJECT PHASE TOPOLOGY
NO ACTIVE OR DELAYED PHASE IS CONFIGURED

“Canonical stage”, “template provenance” and “phase topology” are engineering words. A designer reading them concludes something is broken and that she broke it. Worse, they survive into Care: a fully settled project still shows the classification complaint and still nags This project does not have a designated decision lead yet.

The same leak, in motion

On a cold load, every band fetches independently and each announces itself in its own bespoke italic string — no skeleton, no spinner, no shared rhythm. Seven different loading messages were on screen at once. Unfolding a settled Brief showed only Opening the brief... for more than three seconds. A first-time reader following a shared link reasonably concludes the page is broken.

Reading approvals…  ·  READING PROJECT WORKFLOW…  ·  RESOLVING THE SCHEDULE…  ·  Reading the work…
Reading the schedule…  ·  Loading working budget…  ·  Loading authorizations…  ·  OPENING THE LEDGER…

Principle violated  ·  speak the user’s language; never expose internal model state as status; one system voice for one system state.

Fix direction

Demote every machine-state notice into a single collapsed “needs setup” affordance on the section header, with a remedy behind it.
04

Creation → install, walked live

The friction timeline

A new engagement was created from scratch in production — client “UX Walk Aug 13”, one room, $25,000–$45,000 band — and driven forward until the walk hit a wall it could not pass without emailing a real human. Four findings here are new; the last one is structural.

  1. Step 01 · Discovery → Direction

    The entry point skips the doc’s own Direction section Medium

    Discovery ends in a clean handoff card — Ready for Direction — essentials captured with BEGIN THE DIRECTION. Clicking it hard-navigates straight out of the document into the Drafting Room proposal editor. The Direction section does exist on the doc — Shape the direction — but the only path anyone actually takes never shows it.

  2. Step 02 · Drafting room · NEW FINDING

    Choosing a client from a picklist fires the invite High

    The client field reads Select or invite a client…. Clicking the row in the dropdown — a row labelled INVITE & LINK — flipped to INVITING… and sent the link immediately. No confirm, no undo, no preview of what the client receives. An irreversible outbound send disguised as a selection gesture, at the exact moment the designer is still deciding whether this deal is real.

    The pattern — send affordances swallowing navigation affordances

    This is not one bad dropdown. An independent walker found the same shape on the desk: the Test Walker card — the invoice-overdue variant — is a single button whose entire surface, project title included, opens the Accounts receivables send-reminder composer. Clicking the title is the universal “open it” gesture, and it is exactly what the sibling Winkys and SMS House cards do. Here it answers the intent “open my project” with “contact your client.” There is no route to the underlying document from that card at all.

    Fairness: the composer does require a further explicit SEND REMINDER click — the trap is at the card, not at the end of it. The picklist has no such second gate. Together they read as a habit: in this product, the outbound action is claiming the surface that navigation should own.

  3. Step 03 · Drafting room

    “4 of 7 facets written” overstates what is written Minor

    Role rates, rates & ceiling, retainer and terms all still needed manual entry, and the client copy meanwhile advertised DESIGN AUTHORIZATION CEILING   $0 and $0 · agreement activates immediately to a live preview pane.

  4. Step 04 · Back to the document · NEW FINDING

    The document URL breaks permanently the moment Direction starts High

    The engagement lived at /doc/597e1166… through Brief and Discovery. Once Direction began, the canonical document silently became /doc/daa68058… — the proposal’s id. The original URL, and its entry in the ⌘K recents list, now return an error. Every bookmark, every link pasted into a thread, every browser-history entry captured before Direction is a dead link forever.

    Reproduced twice within this walk — and then independently reproduced a third time by a second session, from a different path entirely: on a separate lead (“Fable UX Walk”), pressing Save agreement itself errored to the same No document answers to this name. Two sessions, two entry paths, one break at the same Direction boundary. This is the highest-confidence defect in the deck.

  5. Step 05 · People room · NEW FINDING

    A draft agreement is reported to the studio as sent High

    The agreement was only ever saved — the send modal was explicitly backed out of. The People room nonetheless renders the relationship as a proposal in flight and prompts the designer to go chase it. Nurture logic is reading draft existence as outbound activity, which means the studio gets told to nudge clients who have never received anything.

    NURTURE   Proposal out — a nudge or a call may be overdue.   [ REACH OUT ]
    …while the journey entry immediately to its left reads Proposal drafted — UX Walk Aug 13.
  6. Step 06 · The wall

    There is no designer-side path to a signed agreement High

    At 7 of 7 facets and Ready to send · every contractual facet is present. the only doors out are Send later and Send agreement → — a real email to a real client. There is no mark-as-signed, no simulate-acceptance, no sandbox. The walk backed out via PUT BACK · ESC and stopped there; project and install phases could not be reached on a new engagement at all.

    As a QA blocker: nobody can dry-run this product end to end. Every rehearsal of the signed→project→install path costs a real send to a real address, which is why the install-phase evidence in this deck comes from pre-existing reference projects rather than from the walk.

    As a product observation: the same wall faces the designer. Phase never advances on anything but a countersigned agreement — the rail sat at Direction DRAFTING, Proposal – with the document complete — so a studio cannot walk a prospective client through what the book will look like, cannot train a new hire on a fake job, and cannot recover from a client who signs on paper. One escape hatch (“record a signature received outside Patina”) resolves the blocker and a real workflow at once.

Also seen, smaller

The visible FIND ANYTHING ⌘K control scrolls the page instead of opening the command bar — only the literal keyboard chord works, so the one discoverable entry point to the portal’s only global navigation is inert to the mouse. RELEASE FOR AUTHORIZATION gives no feedback at all when nothing is eligible. The IN HAND timer kept billing time to Winkys after navigating into a different document. Cold loads of a doc URL land mid-scroll, so a first-time viewer following a shared link never sees the header or the phase spine. And the desk carries three separate Capture a lead affordances on one screen.

Worth saying plainly

Much of this product is very good, and the critique is only legible against that. The “Draw an invoice” composer is genuinely well built and cancels cleanly. The sheet overlays — call sheet, accounts — behave correctly and consistently under PUT BACK · ESC. Escaping back to the desk with the gold recently-visited ring is a lovely piece of orientation, and the empty states are the best-written copy in the portal. The problems in this deck are compositional, not craft.

05

Assessment

Install week, demanded vs. mounted

Install is the week with trucks, crews, damaged goods, a client standing in the room, and the last money in the engagement. Here is what that week asks of a document, against what the document currently provides.

  • 01 Room-by-room state “Primary bedroom: 8 of 11 placed, 2 damaged, 1 not shipped” is the question on install day. Install does not even offer the flat line-item table it had in project phase — the room grouping is dropped and the whole schedule collapses to 0 OF 1 INSTALLED · BILL 1 UNINVOICED with no controls. The designer does the grouping in her head, on site, holding a phone. Largest single gap in the composition. Critical
  • 02 Punch as a first-class band Punch is generated during the walkthrough and it gates final payment — yet it has no band, only coordination rows nested inside the schedule. Major
  • 03 A forcing function at close Harper Vale proves there is none: closing was a state change, not a checklist that had to clear. Uninstalled and uninvoiced items walk straight out of the system. This one costs cash. Critical
  • 04 Care held back until close clears The single structural signal that the doc is in install — the Care band unfolding — points at the phase after install. The one compositional change install makes is to foreground what comes next. Major
  • 05 A working surface, not a scroll tail Install sits at the bottom of a long page beneath read-only recaps of brief, discovery and direction plus the permanently empty mood-board and plan-room bands: the worst signal-to-scroll ratio in the product, at the moment of highest urgency and the worst connectivity. Major
  • 06 Reconciliation across the install/care boundary “Book closed”, “Care ongoing” and an uninstalled item are all displayable at once and never reconciled — T1’s contradiction problem localised to the most expensive seam. Major
  • 07 Unmet entirely Arrival and staging logistics — a time-and-location model, not a specification model — and day structure. A call sheet exists in the product; install never composes one. Gap

Verdict: install is a label on project mode, not a mode. It is the highest-leverage compositional gap in the doc.

Below the cut, still real: BAND $ from – to $0 on unset budgets; Name a phase… still offered after Completion; punch buried inside the schedule (folded into #4). The four journey findings in section 04 are new since this ranking was drawn and belong at roughly ranks 3, 5, 7 and 9.

07

Three proposals

What the doc could be

Three compositions, drawn with the real content of the walked projects. None of them changes the data. Every figure, room, authorization and phase below already exists in the product today; what changes is composition, hierarchy and navigation. They are not exclusive — A and B are the same doc in two modes, and C sits above both.

Layout A

The Spine Rules

One organ owns status. The schedule spine computes it; the header chip and the desk card render that answer verbatim. Everything the machine wants to complain about collapses into one quiet affordance, and money becomes a single region with one figure that matters.

Mock · real Winky figures. The four brand-new elements are the single derived chip, the “needs setup · 2” collapse, the nested money region, and the one-line collapse of never-populated bands.

Why

  • T1 — one organ computes status; the chip is a render of the spine, so the contradiction has nowhere to live. The desk card would read the same string.
  • T6 — NO ACTIVE OR DELAYED PHASE IS CONFIGURED and NO TEMPLATE PROVENANCE RECORDED become two entries behind Needs setup · 2, each with a remedy.
  • T3 — one region, one dominant figure, three subordinate tiers in dependency order. The accounts strip stops being a fifth peer that disagrees.
  • T5 — four permanently-empty bands become one quiet line that still offers the door.
  • #5 in the ranking — a project with no schedule composed now has an unavoidably blank status organ instead of a confident-looking chip.

Trade-off

Everything now depends on the schedule being composed — the spine becomes a hard prerequisite rather than one section among many, so a studio that skips it gets a doc that visibly refuses to state a status.

Layout B

Install Is a Room Problem

The same document, in a mode it does not currently have. Organised by room and by day rather than by line item, with punch as a peer band and closing as a gate that can refuse. Care does not appear until the gate clears.

Care opens when this gate clears — not before.

Mock · Winky rooms plus the real Harper Vale close-out failure ($3,200 chair, 1 uninvoiced bill) shown as what it should have been: a gate that refuses.

Why

  • T2, install demand #1 — the room axis is the composition, so “8 of 11 placed, 2 damaged, 1 not shipped” is read, not reconstructed on site.
  • T2, demand #3 — close becomes a checklist that can refuse. Harper Vale’s $3,200 chair and uninvoiced bill would have physically blocked the button that was pressed.
  • Install demand #2 — punch is a peer band with its own count, not coordination rows hidden inside a schedule accordion.
  • Install demands #4 and #5 — Care is locked behind the gate rather than unfolding as install’s only signal, and the recap tail folds into the rail so the working surface is the top of the page.
  • The strip-down — install currently deletes the authority band, budget grid and authorizations ledger. Here they fold rather than vanish, so a designer standing in the room can still answer “is this line authorized?” without leaving the phase.
  • Unmet-entirely list — the day strip gives install a time-and-location model, which the existing call sheet feature can already populate.

Trade-off

A hard close gate will trap real studios on messy jobs — the client who never takes the last chair still has to be closable, so the gate needs an explicit, logged override rather than none at all.

Layout C

The Shelf

A tier above the doc. Every engagement as one spine-state row — phase, week, and what is missing. The desk’s triage cards stay, but as exceptions over the list rather than instead of it. One glance answers “what is the state of my book?”

Sorted by the spine · every row is one active_section value — no second computation, no new data.

Mock · six of these rows are the engagements actually visible in the account on 13 Aug; the install-phase row (“Lakeshore Library & Lounge”) is invented to show the phase filter doing work — the only real doc that crossed install is Harper Vale, already in Care.

Why

  • T4 — the portfolio question finally has a page, and “show me everything in install” is one filter click.
  • T4, second order — “no schedule composed” becomes a visible cell rather than a condition nothing ever renders. Hollow projects can no longer hide behind a confident desk card.
  • T1 — every row is one active_section value, so the roster cannot disagree with the doc it links to.
  • Ranking #10 — REVEAL 3 MORE FOLIOS is retired; breadth is the shelf’s job, and the desk keeps only depth.
  • T2 at a distance — the money-at-risk column makes an uninvoiced $3,200 visible from the roster, weeks after the doc that owns it stopped being opened.

Trade-off

It reintroduces a list-and-detail hierarchy that R21 deliberately dissolved — the shelf is a second home screen, and two front doors need a very clear division of labour or the desk quietly dies.

08

Close

What we’d validate next

  1. Recapture the send wall with a real test send. Complete the walk past Send agreement → to a controlled address, countersign, and capture the full signed→project→install path on a document created from scratch. Everything after step 06 in section 04 is currently inferred from reference projects, not walked.
  2. Reproduce the URL break a third time, deliberately. Confirm whether the pre-Direction id is dead or merely unlinked, and whether a redirect is possible — that determines if this is a one-line fix or a data question.
  3. Instrument the picklist invite, and audit the desk card with it. Find out how many invites in production were fired by a selection gesture rather than a send gesture, and how many receivables composers were opened by someone who meant to open a project. Those two numbers decide the severity of the whole send-swallows-navigation pattern.
  4. Re-test RESOLVE THE SCHEDULE deliberately, with the network log open. One trial showed no visible response; that is medium confidence and it is the most prominent action on the page, so it deserves either a bug or a dismissal.
  5. Trace the room breadcrumb. Confirm the ← THE DOCUMENT link resolves through the room’s canonical doc rather than the held document, and decide what should happen when a room legitimately belongs to two projects.
  6. Walk install on a real install week with a designer on site, on a phone, on bad wifi. Every claim in section 05 is a desk inference; the room-axis proposal deserves one live test before it is built.
